theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What name is given to the planned process of putting right a service failure and winning back the guest's goodwill?
Name the chart that ranks causes from largest to smallest, often used to find the "vital few" types of guest complaint.
A hotel had 18 complaints in a month when it sold 3,600 room nights. How many complaints is that per 1,000 room nights?
What term describes giving front-line staff the authority to solve guest problems without first asking a manager?
What is the name for a person who uses a hotel as an ordinary guest and reports on the service against a checklist?
Which diagram, also named after Ishikawa, groups the possible causes of a service problem under main headings?
A hotel's guest satisfaction score rose from 80% to 86%. By how many percentage points did it rise?
Name the service quality model built on reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness.
Give the three-letter abbreviation for a written document that sets out, step by step, how a task such as check-in must be done.
What term is used for colleagues and departments who receive a service from others inside the hotel, such as housekeeping receiving linen from the laundry?
A hotel's target is to reply to 95% of online reviews within 48 hours. Last month it replied to 114 of 120 reviews in time. What percentage did it achieve?
What name is given to the record a hotel keeps of a returning guest's past stays and preferences?
On a day with 80 arrivals, 72 rooms were ready by the hotel's 3:00 p.m. standard. What percentage of rooms met the standard?
Give the three-letter abbreviation for guests who receive special pre-arrival checks and a senior manager's welcome.

essays.stem: You are the new guest services manager at a 150-room hotel in Montego Bay. Plan how you would set and roll out service standards for the front office, housekeeping and the restaurant.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by finding out what guests expect, using the last six months of surveys, online reviews and complaint logs, and by asking the heads of front office, housekeeping and the restaurant what problems they see. Next I would map the guest journey and list the main contact points, such as reservations, arrival, room readiness, meals and checkout. For each point I would write a few clear, measurable standards with the department heads and some front-line staff, for example: answer the phone within three rings, rooms released by 3:00 p.m., food served within 20 minutes of ordering. I would check the standards are realistic for our staffing and budget. To roll them out, I would train each team using short sessions and role plays, put the standards into SOPs and checklists, and launch them at shift briefings. I would then monitor results through system data, spot checks and mystery guest visits, share the results each month, recognise good performance and review the standards every six months.
markingPoints: Bases the standards on evidence of guest expectations (surveys, reviews, complaints)
Involves department heads and front-line staff in writing the standards
Writes clear, measurable standards for the main contact points
Rolls out through training, SOPs and briefings
Monitors, gives feedback, recognises staff and reviews the standards

essays.stem: A hotel's complaint log for last quarter shows 210 complaints: 84 about room cleanliness, 63 about slow check-in, 30 about noise, 21 about Wi-Fi and 12 about food. Analyse the figures and recommend where management should act first, with reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: Room cleanliness makes up 84 of 210 complaints, or 40%, and slow check-in 63 of 210, or 30%. Together these two types make up 70% of all complaints, so they are the "vital few" that a Pareto analysis points to. Noise is about 14%, Wi-Fi 10% and food about 6%. I would act on cleanliness and check-in first, because fixing them would remove most complaints and they affect almost every guest. The two may also be linked: if rooms are not cleaned and released on time, guests wait longer at check-in. I would hold a root-cause session with housekeeping and front office, using a fishbone diagram to look at staffing, methods, equipment and supplies, and I would check room release times in the system. Actions might include changing housekeeping shift times, a room inspection checklist and a faster check-in process. I would set targets, such as halving these complaints next quarter, and still assign owners to the smaller issues, especially Wi-Fi, which may be a cheap fix.
markingPoints: Works out the shares correctly (40% and 30%, together 70%)
Identifies cleanliness and check-in as the priority, using Pareto reasoning
Notes the possible link between room readiness and check-in delays
Recommends root-cause analysis before choosing actions
Sets targets and does not ignore the smaller complaint types

essays.stem: Describe a service recovery procedure for a villa company, from the moment a guest complains to the follow-up after the guest has gone home.
essays.modelAnswer: When a guest complains, the staff member who hears it owns it until it is solved or passed on. They listen without interrupting, thank the guest for raising it and apologise sincerely for the experience, without blaming others. They confirm the facts and ask what the guest would like to happen. They then act quickly: fix the problem if they can, within their empowerment limit, for example a credit of up to J$15,000, or call the villa manager at once if it is bigger. The guest is told what will happen and by when. The manager checks back with the guest the same day to confirm they are satisfied. Every complaint is recorded in the complaint log with the date, type, cause, action and cost. After the guest leaves, the manager sends a personal message thanking them and saying what has been changed. Each month the manager analyses the log for patterns, reviews whether the compensation was fair and consistent, and uses the findings in training.
markingPoints: Listen, thank and apologise sincerely without blaming others
Act quickly within clear empowerment limits, or escalate
Confirm the outcome with the guest and follow up after departure
Record every complaint in a log
Analyse the log for patterns and use it to improve and train

essays.stem: Compare three methods a hotel can use to gather guest feedback, and recommend a suitable mix for a 30-room boutique hotel.
essays.modelAnswer: Post-stay email surveys are cheap and give numbers that can be tracked over time, but response rates are often low and the hotel learns about problems only after the guest has left. Online reviews are public and influence future bookings, so they must be watched; however, they come mostly from very happy or very unhappy guests and are not a balanced sample. Mystery guest visits test the standards against a checklist and show how staff behave when no manager is watching, but they cost money and give only a snapshot of one or two stays. A fourth option is an in-stay check, where a manager asks guests during the stay how things are going; this lets problems be fixed before departure. For a 30-room boutique hotel I would recommend in-stay checks by the duty manager, a short post-stay survey and daily monitoring of reviews, with a mystery guest visit once or twice a year. This mix is affordable, catches problems early and gives both numbers and detail.
markingPoints: Describes at least three methods accurately
Gives a strength and a weakness of each method
Notes the value of catching problems during the stay
Makes a clear recommendation suited to a small hotel and its budget
Justifies the mix (cost, timeliness, balance of numbers and detail)

essays.stem: Evaluate the benefits and risks of letting front-line staff offer compensation to unhappy guests, and explain how you would control the risks.
essays.modelAnswer: The main benefit is speed: the guest's problem is solved by the first person they speak to, which reduces anger, saves managers' time and often turns a bad experience into a good one. Staff also feel trusted, which can raise morale and pride in service. The risks are that staff may give too much or too little, treat similar guests differently, give away compensation to avoid effort, or be pressured by demanding guests. There is also a risk of fraud if credits are not checked. To control these risks I would set clear limits by role, for example up to J$15,000 for front desk agents and more for supervisors, and give guidelines on what is fair for common problems. Staff would be trained with role plays. Every credit would be logged with the reason, and a manager would review the log each week. Patterns would be discussed with staff in coaching, not used to punish honest mistakes. I conclude that the benefits outweigh the risks if the controls are in place.
markingPoints: Explains the benefits for guests, managers and staff
Identifies the main risks (inconsistency, overspending, pressure, fraud)
Proposes limits by role and guidelines for common problems
Includes training, logging and regular review
Reaches a justified overall judgement

essays.stem: A Negril resort's average online review score has fallen from 4.5 to 3.9 out of 5 in six months. Explain how you would investigate the fall and respond to it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would read all the reviews from the six months and group the comments by theme, such as room condition, food, staff attitude and value for money, and by date, to see when the fall started. I would compare this with our complaint log, survey results, occupancy and any changes we made, such as new suppliers, staff cuts or building work. This should show whether one or two issues are driving the fall. I would then meet the department heads to find the root causes and agree actions with owners and dates. At the same time I would make sure every review gets a polite, personal reply within 48 hours that thanks the guest, accepts fair points and says what has been fixed, without arguing or sharing private details. I would not ask for fake reviews, but I would invite satisfied guests to share their views. I would track the score, the themes and our response time monthly, and report progress to the general manager.
markingPoints: Analyses reviews by theme and date to find when and why the score fell
Cross-checks with other data (complaints, surveys, changes made)
Finds root causes and agrees actions with owners and dates
Replies to reviews professionally and honestly, never using fake reviews
Monitors the score and themes and reports progress

essays.stem: Explain how a general manager can build and keep a strong service culture among hotel staff.
essays.modelAnswer: A service culture is the shared belief among staff that caring for guests is everyone's job. The general manager builds it first by example: being visible in guest areas, greeting guests and staff, and handling problems calmly. Recruitment matters, so the hotel should hire for a positive attitude as well as skills, and induction should explain the hotel's service values and standards. Staff need the tools and training to deliver good service, including clear standards, regular coaching and the authority to solve guest problems. Communication keeps the culture alive: daily briefings, sharing guest comments, and listening to staff ideas. Recognition is powerful, for example naming staff praised by guests at briefings, an employee of the month award and thanks from managers. The manager should also look after internal service between departments, because staff who are treated well treat guests well. Finally, service results should be measured and discussed openly, and poor service should be dealt with fairly and quickly so standards are not seen as optional.
markingPoints: Leads by example and is visible
Recruits for attitude and inducts staff in service values
Trains, coaches and empowers staff
Communicates and recognises good service
Measures service and deals with poor service fairly

essays.stem: Describe the measures you would report each month to a hotel's owners on guest service quality, and explain why each one matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I would report a small set of key performance indicators, each against its target and last year's figure. The guest satisfaction score from post-stay surveys matters because it shows how guests rated the whole stay. The average online review score matters because future guests read it before booking. The complaint rate per 1,000 room nights matters because it allows fair comparison between busy and quiet months, and I would show the top complaint types and their trend. The share of complaints solved at first contact shows how well staff are empowered. Repeat guest percentage shows loyalty, which is cheaper than finding new guests. I would also report the cost of service recovery, so owners can see what poor service costs, and the results of any mystery guest visit against the standards. For each measure I would explain the cause of any big change and the action planned. The report should be short, use charts, and protect guest and staff privacy by not naming individuals.
markingPoints: Chooses relevant measures such as satisfaction, review score and complaint rate
Explains why each measure matters to the owners
Shows results against targets and trends, using fair comparisons
Explains causes and planned actions
Keeps the report concise and protects privacy

essays.stem: Explain how a hotel can meet the needs of guests with disabilities, older guests and guests from different cultures, while keeping its service standards consistent.
essays.modelAnswer: The hotel's standards should set the same level of respect and care for every guest, while allowing staff to adjust how they deliver it. For guests with disabilities, the reservations team should ask about needs before arrival and confirm what the hotel can offer, such as an accessible room, ramp access or visual alarms. Staff should be trained to offer help without taking over, and to speak to the guest, not their companion. The hotel should check its accessible facilities regularly and describe them honestly in its advertising. Older guests may value rooms near lifts, clear signs and a slower, patient pace, but staff should not assume they need help. For guests from different cultures, staff can learn about likely preferences, such as food needs, religious practices and language, and the hotel can provide translated information. In every case staff should ask rather than assume, and treat each guest as an individual. Feedback from these guests should be reviewed to improve the standards.
markingPoints: Keeps one standard of respect while adapting delivery to the guest
Gives suitable actions for guests with disabilities (pre-arrival checks, facilities, training)
Gives suitable actions for older guests without stereotyping
Gives suitable actions for guests from other cultures (food, faith, language)
Uses feedback from these guests to improve

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan to keep guest service quality high at a resort during the December-to-April peak season, when occupancy is above 90%.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start planning in September by looking at last season's complaints, survey scores and staffing records to see where service slipped. I would forecast occupancy and arrivals week by week and plan staffing to match, recruiting and training seasonal staff early and pairing them with experienced colleagues. Leave would be planned so key staff are available. I would check that supplies such as linen, guest amenities and food are ordered in time, and that equipment such as lifts, air conditioning and kitchen machines is serviced before December. Busy points such as check-in and checkout would get extra cover, and the front office and housekeeping would agree room release times. Standards would stay the same, but I would brief staff daily on arrivals, VIPs and known issues. Managers would be visible in guest areas at peak times. I would watch complaints, review scores and waiting times weekly so problems are fixed fast, and I would look after staff wellbeing with fair rotas and breaks, since tired staff give poorer service.
markingPoints: Uses last season's data and forecasts demand
Plans staffing, recruitment, training and leave early
Prepares supplies and equipment before the season
Keeps standards, briefs staff daily and monitors results weekly
Protects staff wellbeing during the busy period

practical1.title: Analyse a hotel complaint log and present a service improvement plan
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a 100-room hotel on the north coast with a three-month complaint log (about 150 entries), its guest survey results and its current service standards. As a group, analyse the complaints and prepare a service improvement plan for the general manager. Each member has a named role: data analyst (sorts the complaints by type and department in a spreadsheet, works out the complaint rate per 1,000 room nights and draws a Pareto chart, checking every figure twice); root-cause lead (leads the group through a fishbone diagram for the biggest complaint type and records the likely causes); standards writer (rewrites one service standard or SOP so it is clear and measurable); action planner (writes the improvement plan with actions, owners, dates, a cost in J$ and the measures that will show success); and presenter (presents the findings and plan to the assessor, acting as general manager, in 10 minutes). In a group of four, the action planner also presents. Every member must answer at least one question from the assessor.
materials: Case pack from the assessor: complaint log, survey results, current standards, room nights sold
Computers with spreadsheet, word processing and presentation software
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The sorted complaint data and the Pareto chart on screen
The fishbone diagram on the flipchart with the likely causes marked
The rewritten service standard or SOP
The written improvement plan with owners, dates, costs and measures
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Complaint shares and the rate per 1,000 room nights are correct and were checked twice
Identified the priority complaint types from the Pareto analysis
Root causes are supported by the data, not guessed
The rewritten standard is clear, measurable and realistic
The plan has actions, owners, dates, costs and success measures
Explained and defended the plan when questioned
safety: Treat the case data as confidential guest information; use made-up names only and return all printouts
Write about service problems and processes, not about individual staff members' character
Respect each other's views and share the workload fairly
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Role-play service recovery and write the hotel's empowerment guideline
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group three guest complaint cases from a made-up villa company or resort, for example a family whose room was not ready at 6:00 p.m., a guest whose airport transfer did not arrive, and a guest who posted an angry review after a noisy night. Part A (about 1 hour 15 minutes): role-play each case. In each round one member plays the front-line staff member, one the guest (using the assessor's role card), one the duty manager who is called in when the guest is still unhappy, and one the observer, who scores the recovery on a checklist (listen, apologise, act, confirm, follow up, record). In a group of five, the fifth member records each case in a complaint log. Rotate the roles so every member handles a guest at least once. Part B (about 1 hour 15 minutes): as a group, write a one-page empowerment guideline that sets the compensation limits for each role in J$, what is fair for common problems, and how credits are logged and reviewed; and write a public reply to the angry online review. Each member drafts one section, and the group agrees the final version.
materials: Complaint case cards and guest role cards from the assessor
Observer checklist and complaint log templates
A table and chairs set up as a front desk or lounge
Computer and printer, or flipchart paper and markers
photos: A role-play in progress at the set-up front desk (faces only if all agree)
The observer checklists completed for each round
The complaint log entries for the three cases
The final empowerment guideline with the limits for each role
The written reply to the online review
checklist: Listened, apologised sincerely and did not blame others when playing the staff role
Offered a fair, realistic remedy within the agreed limit, or escalated correctly
Stayed calm and respectful with an angry guest
Recorded the complaint accurately and agreed a follow-up
Drafted a clear section of the empowerment guideline with sensible J$ limits
Helped write a professional, honest public reply that protects guest privacy
Gave or received observer feedback constructively
safety: Use only the made-up cases; do not discuss real guests or real workplaces
Keep role-play notes and logs confidential to the group and the assessor
Keep the role plays respectful, and stop if anyone becomes uncomfortable
Photograph faces only if every person agrees and the Centre allows it
